what_it_does: This paper describes a specialized chip that solves pathfinding problems (like finding the shortest route for a robot through a maze or finding where to route signals on a circuit board) much faster and with less power than traditional digital computers. The innovation replaces normal logic circuits with compute-in-memory (CIM) architecture—where data processing happens directly where the data is stored instead of shuttling bits back and forth to distant memory. The authors improve CIM efficiency in two ways: (1) they use a bidirectional search strategy that explores paths from both start and goal simultaneously, using the full processing time more efficiently; and (2) they replace power-hungry flip-flop memory cells with a dynamic-logic design that uses less area and leakage. The result is a 32-by-32 macro that consumes just 69.4 femtojoules per computation step (extremely low energy) and completes each step in 0.22 nanoseconds.
